title: Review 80: Region Focused Analysis
author: Chris Jones
summary: This weekly review from Chris Jones of the SMARTcurriculum Network presents Paper 2 of a regional series, a Manchester-focused analysis of Education Action Zones, local deprivation and educational reform. Manchester was one of the original 25 EAZs launched in 1998, with about 1 million pounds a year, community services placed in schools, extended learning time and early ICT use. Jones traces early gains in attendance and literacy, uneven progress afterward, and a mixed 2026 picture in which some inner-city secondaries beat national averages while north Manchester still lags. He describes how multi-academy trusts and the local authority now coordinate schools, and he outlines the Greater Manchester skills strategy under Andy Burnham as a devolved, place-based model. His strategic lessons favour capacity-building over autonomy, sustained intervention, curriculum alignment, stable leadership pipelines and data-driven resourcing. A comparison with Amsterdam, Copenhagen, Berlin and Paris concludes that Manchester's success depends on deepening devolution from coordination to genuine system control.
points: The Manchester EAZ paired roughly 1 million pounds a year with community services in schools and longer learning time, but short-term programmes lacked the structural alignment to transform the system.
Gains have been stronger where trusts, the local authority and community organisations align, which Jones calls coherent system architecture.
The Burnham skills strategy treats skills as economic and social infrastructure linked to transport, housing and health, though school accountability and funding remain nationally controlled.
Five lessons are offered: capacity-building over autonomy, sustained intervention, curriculum aligned to local context, stable leadership pipelines and data-led resource allocation.
Against Amsterdam and Copenhagen (municipal control), Berlin (state level) and Paris (centralised), Manchester sits in between, so devolution must deepen to move from coordination to control.
quotes: The city’s experience underscores a central lesson for future policy: short-term programmes, however innovative, cannot substitute for coherent, embedded system design aligned to local context and need.
Gains have been stronger where MATs, LA, and community organisations align, highlighting the importance of coherent system architecture.
Overall, Burnham’s approach represents a shift toward a territorial education model—one that treats skills as an economic and social infrastructure.
Capacity-building trumps autonomy: Local innovation alone cannot overcome structural disadvantage.
Skills policy is connected to transport, housing, and health strategies, recognising that barriers to learning are often structural rather than purely educational.

Unlike Amsterdam or Copenhagen, Manchester does not fully control its education system; unlike Paris, it has greater scope for local innovation; and unlike Berlin, it lacks a fully embedded federal structure for sustained equity funding.
Future reform should combine the experimental spirit of EAZs with the structural advantages of MAT governance and data-informed planning to tackle persistent inequality.
